Protocol Architecture

Post-Quantum Nostr Proposed as Soft Fork: Quantum Signatures Packed into Legacy Envelopes

By embedding quantum-resistant keys and signatures within reserved event tags, clients and relays can transition asynchronously without breaking legacy software or requiring coordinated protocol upgrades.

By The Observer Cryptography Desk · Sourced from nomadshiba | XBT

In an architectural proposal published to the network Monday, developer nomadshiba outlined a pathway to prepare Nostr for the post-quantum cryptographic transition without fracturing the network or forcing coordinated relay migrations. As nomadshiba framed the proposal: Post-quantum signatures can be added to Nostr as a soft fork inside today's event format, so no client or relay has to upgrade at the same time.

Rather than replacing elliptic curve cryptography in a single disruptive break, the scheme packages two identities and two cryptographic commitments into each transmission: Every event is two events by two different authors, packed into one. An outer legacy envelope preserves existing secp256k1 signatures and standard NIP-01 structures, allowing legacy relays and un-upgraded clients to route and render notes without modification. Within reserved tags, an inner quantum-resistant payload carries an independent public key and a post-quantum signature.

Upgraded clients query legacy relays using a single-letter index tag, rebuild the post-quantum event from the inner envelope, and verify both cryptographic proofs. Crucially, the approach separates relay readiness from client adoption: The goal for now isn't upgrading relays. It's making sure they already have the new forms, so they're ready to switch. Relays that already store legacy events can extract and index the quantum forms at any point in the future.

The decoupling means migration happens on an individual timeline rather than an arbitrary flag day: Nobody has to agree on a date for this. Every client and relay switches when it wants, and each one is safe from the moment it does. Should secp256k1 ever be broken by quantum computing hardware, clients already operating in dual mode can prune legacy envelopes entirely, preserving social graphs and identities that established their post-quantum keys ahead of time.

Grassroots & Sovereign Media

The Printed Web: Nostr Community Zine Brings Sovereign Social Protocols to Paper

Sourced from No Good Kid and AJ

While protocol developers design quantum fallbacks in code, a parallel grassroots effort is returning sovereign communication to physical newsprint and photocopiers. Creator No Good Kid published printable templates and layout guides for a physical pamphlet designed for offline distribution, declaring: Nostr Community Zine is meant to be printed and shared at local meetups and regional conferences.

The physical tactile artifact was accompanied by folding demonstrations that drew admiration for precise workshop discipline. Community observer AJ noted the exacting finish of the folded broadsheets: Clean, straight lines—a stark contrast to the wonky leaflets that often litter conference registration tables. The initiative highlights a recurring theme across sovereign technology communities: high-tech peer-to-peer protocols often find their most enduring evangelism through durable, hands-on physical artifacts.

Security & Infrastructure

Scattered Patch-Now Wave Hits Gateways, Routers, and Wallets

Sourced from Freedom.Tech

Infrastructure review service Freedom.Tech documented an urgent batch of updates spanning four distinct operational layers: Four releases carried Patch now severity this week, covering distinct attack surfaces rather than one shared vulnerability class, including the openclaw Lightning gateway, StartOS router admin software, Bisq peer-to-peer exchange client, and ZEUS mobile wallets.

While none of the releases published immediate public CVE references, None listed CVEs directly, but the Bisq release stems from a formal security audit. Alongside point fixes, self-hosters faced breaking architecture shifts as BorgBackup 2.0 and Gitea 28.0.0 both crossed major-version boundaries.
